title: The Smiling Well
premise: Rafael Sterling returns to the family house to bury her twin brother Rafe, only to discover at the funeral that the body in the casket is hers — and that everyone, including their mother, seems to believe she is the one who died. The mirrors in the house begin lagging a second behind reality, and in that stolen second Rafael glimpses what was invited in decades ago by an ancestor's bargain: an inheritance passed twin to twin, paid in identity. As the lag widens and the thing wearing her face grows more solid, she must uncover which Sterling made the pact, refuse the inheritance aloud before sunrise, and choose whether survival means erasing herself — or letting the well keep its original debtor.
about_author: Tamsin Almeida is the pen name of a former archivist who spent nine years cataloguing estate papers in coastal New England, where she developed a professional unease about family records that end too neatly. She writes horror about houses that remember, and claims she has never once looked into an antique mirror after midnight — on principle.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She arrives home for her brother Rafe's funeral, exhausted and grieving, and finds the open casket bearing her own face. Her mother calls her 'Rafe' without hesitation and hands her the eulogy for 'Rafael.' The chapter establishes her compulsive documentation habit as she photographs everything, unable to look away from the corpse. Emotional beat: vertigo of grief curdling into uncanny denial.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She searches the house for proof of who she is — old photos, school records, her own handwriting — but every artifact now shows two children where there should be twins, or one child with a smudged face. The mirrors behave normally, but she notices the house smells like well water everywhere. Emotional beat: the terror of losing external evidence of self.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, first mirror incident. At 11:47 p.m., the hallway mirror reflects her raising a hand a full second after she does. In the lag, the reflection keeps moving when she stops. She films it; the footage shows nothing wrong. Her mother, downstairs, is heard speaking to someone in the empty kitchen. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Kept Below
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: chapters from a 1948 diary interleaved with Rafael's present. Great-grandmother Odile Sterling writes of a drought, a smiling well on the property, and a bargain: the well returns water if the Sterlings feed it 'the spare' — one of every pair of twins. Rafael realizes Rafe wasn't the sacrifice; she was meant to be. Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as predation.

chapters.title: Mother Knows the Words
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She confronts her mother, who finally speaks plainly: the family has renewed the bargain every generation, and this time the mother chose Rafael — because Rafael left, married out, changed her name, and 'stopped being a Sterling.' Grief and rage collide. The mother recites part of an invocation she refuses to finish. Emotional beat: betrayal inside love.

chapters.title: The Lag Widens
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The mirror delay stretches to five seconds, then ten; reflections begin showing the room as it was decades ago, with a girl standing at the well's edge. Every clock in the house reads different times. Rafael's own reflection starts smiling when she doesn't. She barricades the hallway but hears water running behind walls. Emotional beat: claustrophobic escalation, time itself failing.

chapters.title: The Thing That Smiles
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Rafael and the reflection. The double steps fully out of the glass during a blackout, wearing Rafael's memories fluently but getting small things wrong — the wrong scar, the wrong first kiss. It argues gently that it has wanted to be real all along, and that Rafael has always felt like the copy. Emotional beat: seductive horror; identity questioned from within.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. In Odile's diary's final pages she finds the escape clause: the debt can be refused aloud at the well's mouth before dawn, but refusal requires naming oneself truly — and the well will try to make her doubt which name is hers. The mother, weeping, reveals she once refused it herself and lost her own twin sister to it. Emotional beat: desperate clarity, stakes fully understood.

chapters.title: At the Mouth of the Well
chapters.summary: Climax. Rafael descends to the well with the double following, both claiming the same name, while the mother holds the flashlight and the diary. As the sky grays, Rafael refuses the inheritance — not by denying the double, but by claiming her whole flawed life aloud, mistakes included, which the double cannot copy. The well takes the oldest debt instead: the mother steps forward and finishes the invocation reversed, offering herself. Emotional beat: sacrificial climax, identity won through specificity.

chapters.title: Everything Documented
chapters.summary: Resolution, weeks later. Rafael buries the casket properly relabeled, sells the house, and donates Odile's diary to an archive with a warning letter attached. The final scene: in a motel bathroom far away, the mirror reflects her perfectly, instantly — except for one frame, one morning, where it smiles a half-second early. She documents it, closes the notebook, and drives on. Emotional beat: uneasy peace; memory and identity survive, but never entirely clean.
